# Another Life
URL: https://another-life.dk/

Made for this life. And another.
Hospitality furniture in reclaimed teak. Danish design, made by hand in Indonesia and built to stay in use.

Teak reclaimed from houses, bridges and boats across Indonesia. Where our wood comes from
Once a family home in Java
Old joglo pillars, ready for another life.
Once a bridge over a river
Wood that carried people across the water for decades.
Once a fishing boat
Timber recovered from fishing boats.

Seven pieces in reclaimed teak, designed for hospitality.

# Another Life Mission
URL: https://another-life.dk/mission.html

Made for a longer life.
Mission
On this page
Keep what already works · Why we exist · Origin · Beliefs · Design · Where we're heading
Last updated 2026-10-16
Our point of viewKeep what already works.
A glass bottle can be washed and refilled before it needs to be melted down. We apply the same principle to furniture: keep it in use through care, repair and reuse.
PurposeWhy we exist.
We make lasting furniture for hospitality.
Hotels and restaurants invest in a sense of place. Their furniture should be part of it for years to come.
Another Life combines Danish design with reclaimed timber and a construction that allows individual parts to be replaced.
The name
ANOTHER — LIFE.
Old material deserves another life. The furniture we make from it should move between owners and places, staying useful each time.
OriginA family company, born in Bali.
The family behind Another Life.
We moved to Bali partly for Green School. Its ethos of doing better helped shape the company.
Here, we saw an opportunity to make hospitality furniture with a longer useful life.
Founded by Stine Palm and Magnus Palm, Another Life is a family company shaped by a Danish heritage of architects and furniture makers.
BeliefsWhat we hold to.
Keep it in use
Design for longevity, repair and reuse before recycling.
Reclaim first
Work with timber that has already served a purpose.
Make it traceable
Show material origins and explain what we know, supported by records.
Design principlesDanish design, made where the material is.
Simple, functional forms follow a Scandinavian design tradition. We make them by hand in Indonesia, close to the timber and the makers.
Sketches, drawings and a burned sample on the design table.
Designed as a system
Flat-packed components bolt together on site, come apart for moving or storage, and can be replaced individually.
Material with character
Grain and marks of age remain visible wherever strength allows. See <a href="material.html">Material and making</a> for the construction and finish.
Where we're headingPlant. Give back. Collaborate.
Tree planting and community partnerships are goals we are working towards, not programmes we claim to have established.
Feet in the sand, eyes on what comes next.
Plant
For the wood we use, we want to plant new trees, including slow-growing native species like teak and ulin.
Give back
We want to share what we build with the communities behind our furniture: the makers we work with and the places the wood comes from.
Collaborate
We're looking for partners who share the idea: planting projects, NGOs, hotels, architects, makers and community initiatives.
If your project shares these aims, we’d like to hear from you.
Work with us

---

# Material and Making
URL: https://another-life.dk/material.html

Material and making
Timber that already lived once.
The origins, finish and construction of SATU, with reclaimed ulin in development.
On this page
Where our wood comes from · Ironwood · Shou Sugi Ban, our way · Natural oil · Making · Hardware · The sign · Built to be rebuilt · Shipping
Last updated 2026-10-16
Chapter 1 · Where our wood comes fromTimber with a history.
Old wood waiting outside the workshop.
Much of our teak comes from old joglos, traditional Javanese houses with tall roofs supported by four main pillars and timber joinery.
As these buildings are dismantled, we recover timber for another use.
SATU uses reclaimed teak (Tectona grandis) from houses, bridges, boats and other structures. The live Another Life Passport connects the furniture with its recorded origins.
Old posts and beams, marked and sorted before they are cut.
Why origin mattersLook beyond the word reclaimed.
Documented origins help distinguish reclaimed timber from newly harvested wood. The research below explains why sourcing matters.
What the research shows · Logging and land use
01Gaveau and colleagues mapped approximately 272,000 km of primary logging roads built on Borneo between 1973 and 2010.
02Their research highlights the importance of protecting logged forests from fire and conversion to plantations.
03By 2010, industrial oil-palm and timber plantations covered about 10% of Borneo. These findings describe regional land-use change, not the origin of any individual teak batch.
And teak?Age affects teak properties.
A 2018 study compared 10-year-old, short-rotation teak with 40-year-old, long-rotation teak:
Heartwood, the durable core
10 years≈ 40%
40 years≈ 80%
Density
10 years472 kg/m³
40 years664 kg/m³
The younger wood was also less resistant to decay in the study. These results describe the tested timber, not measured performance of SATU. Reclaimed structural teak lets us work with older timber that is already available.
Research on reuse23–92%
Lower climate impact across reuse scenarios in a study of a wooden house.
A 2024 study in Buildings reported 23–92% lower global warming potential than its reference scenario, depending on the extent of reuse. This is building research, not a carbon assessment of our furniture.
Our woodFrom former use to furniture.
A joglo: the Javanese teak house much of our wood comes from.
We select timber that has already served in a house, bridge, boat or other structure.
The Passport connects the recorded history with the furniture:
Its former use and source.
Records for its batch.
The code on the piece.
Open an example passportHow the Passport works
Sources: Gaveau et al., Four decades of forest persistence, clearance and logging on Borneo, PLoS ONE 2014 · Gaveau et al., Reconciling forest conservation and logging in Indonesian Borneo, PLoS ONE 2013 · Carbon assessment of a wooden single-family building, Buildings 2024 · Rizanti et al., Comparison of teak wood properties: short versus long rotation, Annals of Forest Science 2018
Chapter 2 · In developmentMeet ulin, Borneo's ironwood.
Reclaimed ulin: weathered outside, warm and dense inside.Old ulin beams. The S-shaped irons keep the ends from splitting.
Ulin (Eusideroxylon zwageri), also known as Borneo ironwood, is a dense, slow-growing timber traditionally used for boats, bridges and waterside structures.
Our first reclaimed-ulin samples have been made. It remains in development as our second material.
Our sourcing approach
We work only with reclaimed ulin, with its origins traced and documented. We do not source newly felled ulin.
Chapter 3 · Shou Sugi Ban, our wayFire, borrowed from Japan.
Burning the surface of the timber.
Yakisugi, often called Shou Sugi Ban, is a Japanese technique traditionally used to char cedar.
We adapt the process for reclaimed teak, darkening the surface with flame and finishing it with natural oil. It brings out the grain and gives SATU its deep colour.
Chapter 4 · Natural oilInto the wood, not on top of it.
Old nail holes and marks stay part of the board.
The finish is part of ongoing care.
Natural oil penetrates the wood. The surface can be re-oiled when it needs care.
Marks from the timber’s first life remain visible wherever they do not compromise strength.
MakingMade in Indonesia.
Every piece is made by hand in Indonesia by makers we work with directly, in small batches.
Producing close to the material keeps the supply chain short and visible.
Stacks of repurposed teak, drilled one board at a time.
The hardwareJoints made to open again.
Three holes, three bolts, at every main joint.
Repair begins with a joint that can be dismantled.
Stainless steel (SUS) bolts screw into threaded inserts set in the wood. The bolts engage with the inserts rather than cutting into the timber, allowing repeated disassembly.
Three-bolt clusters secure the main joints and give SATU its distinctive detail.
The bolt.The insert it screws into.
The sign in the boltsThree dots. One circle.
The three bolts also echo the idea behind Another Life:
Material
The wood already lived once, before it reached our workshop.
Owner
The piece can move on to someone new and keep working.
Place
Undo the bolts and it can be rebuilt somewhere else.
Built to be rebuiltFlat, bolted, and back again.
Parts fit by hand, then bolt together.
Every piece ships flat and bolts together on site.
It can be dismantled for moving, storage or individual component replacement.
ShippingMore chairs in each container.
Flat-packing reduces the space needed for transport.
We estimate a 40 ft high-cube container holds around 1,300 flat-packed chairs, compared with roughly 350 assembled chairs: almost four times as many per load.
Another Life estimates; final capacity depends on packaging and loading. This comparison is not a measured emissions saving.
20 ft40 ft high-cube
Flat-packed · ~1,300Assembled · ~350
Drag the slider to compare. Illustration.

# Another Life Passport
URL: https://another-life.dk/passport.html

Another Life Passport
A story you can scan.
The Another Life Passport is live. Scan the QR code on a piece to see its recorded origins, making, journey and care information.
The code connects each piece to its batch record and stays with the furniture as it moves on.
Last updated 2026-10-16
How it worksScan, explore, care.
Follow a batch of benches through these screens from the live Passport.
01 / 05
01MarkedOne code on every piece.
The system creates a batch code and a QR code, ready for the engraver. The code under the QR is a backup anyone can type in.
02ScannedA guest points a phone at it.
No app. The camera opens the page for that piece, with the batch code at the top.
03Its livesThe whole story in a minute.
Explore the wood’s recorded former life and its route through the workshop to its current setting.
04Its journeyHow far it travelled.
Follow the route from the workshop, with an estimate of transport CO₂ for the piece.
05Its careSomething loose? Tell us.
A short form with a photo comes straight to us, so a small repair keeps the piece in use.
Try itScan the code at the top of this page, or open the example.
Open the example passportFind a piece by its code
Certification and transparencyEvidence that works together.
Independent standards and product records each have a role.
We support FSC’s role in responsible forest sourcing and verified reclaimed material.
Independent certification provides assurance within its scope. The Passport complements that work with records of origin, making, transport and care.
The Passport is our product record, not an independent certification.
For hospitalityA story guests can read for themselves.
Guests can scan the furniture to explore its recorded history and understand the materials around them.
After the first lifeBuilt to support what comes next.
The Passport is already live. Alongside it, we are developing these services to extend the furniture’s useful life:
A chair on the workshop floor, before it is burned.
Replacement parts
A single component, replaced on its own.
Refinishing
A worn surface brought back.
Reconfiguration
Parts rearranged for a new space or use.
Refurbishment
A full restoration of a used piece.
Take-back
Pieces returned to us and given another life, rather than discarded.
Work with usBring the story into your space.
Talk to us about using the live Passport in your hotel or restaurant, or helping develop the next care and reuse services.
Get in touch

# Another Life Questions
URL: https://another-life.dk/faq.html

Questions
Practical answers.
Last updated 2026-10-16
What is Another Life?
Another Life is a Danish family furniture company based in Bali, making reclaimed-teak furniture by hand in Indonesia for hospitality.
What is SATU?
Our first collection comprises seven pieces in reclaimed teak, with a shared flame-darkened finish and bolted construction. See Collection for the full range and dimensions.
What is the furniture made from?
Reclaimed teak, often from old Javanese joglo houses. We retain marks of its former life wherever strength allows. See Material and making for sourcing and finish details.
What is Shou Sugi Ban?
A flame-darkened finish inspired by Japanese yakisugi. We burn the teak surface and finish it with natural oil. See Material and making for the process.
What is ulin?
Borneo ironwood (Eusideroxylon zwageri), a dense, slow-growing timber. Our reclaimed-ulin samples are in development; SATU is made in teak.
How do you approach sustainability?
We prioritise reclaimed timber, repairable construction and efficient packing. Material and making sets out the evidence and its limits; Mission explains our longer-term aims.
What happens when a hotel no longer needs the furniture?
It can be dismantled for storage, moved to a new space or passed to another owner. Take-back and refurbishment services are in development; contact us to discuss a piece.
Is the furniture recyclable?
The bolted construction allows wood and hardware to be separated. Recycling options depend on local facilities and the condition of the materials. We prioritise repair and reuse.
Do you plant trees?
Tree planting and community partnerships are goals, not established programmes. See Mission or contact us about a collaboration.
Can the furniture be used outdoors?
Yes. It is made for hospitality spaces indoors and out, from dining rooms and lobbies to pools, terraces and gardens.
How is the furniture shipped?
Flat-packed for assembly on site. We confirm project options and lead times with your quotation.
What holds the furniture together?
Stainless steel bolts fit into threaded inserts in the wood, with three bolts at each main joint. This allows the joints to be opened and tightened again.
Can the furniture be repaired?
Yes. Individual components can be replaced. Use the Passport repair form to send details and a photograph, or contact us about the part you need.
What is the Another Life Passport?
Our live QR-based product record. Scan the code to explore the piece’s recorded origins, making and journey, find care information or submit a repair enquiry. No app is needed. Visit Passport to try an example.
How much does it cost?
Prices are quoted per project, ex works Indonesia. Send us the pieces, quantities and location for a proposal.
How do I order?
Contact us with your space, the pieces and quantities you need, and your timeline. We’ll reply with options, pricing and lead times.
